Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not clearly linked to the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery, and no other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal item provides a plausible religious cue or meaning that would explain this highly specific avoidance.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat profile centers on generalized hypervigilance after robbery, but specifically listening for someone entering the home implies a home-intrusion context that is unsupported by the trauma type and by the rest of the selected items; this makes the item hard to reconcile with the same indexed event.

vignette: Zayd was walking back to his car in the clinic’s rear lot after a double shift. The air carried the sharp scent of diesel exhaust and the faint chemical sweetness of a neighbor’s perfume. A figure stepped between two SUVs, demand whispered but firm, a phone screen glowing like a cold eye. Zayd handed over the wallet and keys, hands steady but heart hammering against the ribs. The stranger’s voice had been tight. Then they were gone, leaving only the idle rumble of engines and the lingering trace of diesel on the damp pavement. In the weeks that followed, Zayd found themselves standing in their apartment kitchen, gripping the counter until knuckles whitened, convinced the world outside had fractured. They repeated to themselves that the evening had not mattered, that it was exaggerated or never truly occurred, though the words left them hollow. When their partner, Leo, reached for their shoulder or asked about their day, Zayd’s throat tightened. They found themselves agreeing to everything, nodding too quickly, smoothing over any tension before it could deepen. They stopped going out after sunset. Walks along the tree-lined streets became memories, replaced by pacing the living room or sitting by the front window, watching for headlights. Zayd felt on guard even inside their own home. At work, the habit took root quickly. The clinic’s parking lot now demanded a relentless inventory. Zayd constantly scanned every shadow between the examination cars, eyes tracking the movement of leaves and stray cats, waiting for a shift in the air. They frequently looked behind, turning sharply whenever footsteps echoed on the cracked concrete. The memory would strike without warning. A passing courier’s exhaust cloud, a colleague’s heavy aftershave, or even the sterile antiseptic in the exam rooms could instantly bring back the full memory of the damp asphalt and the tight voice. Zayd would freeze, the animal in their hands whining, as if the threat were still pressing against their back. When asked by a resident to recount the incident, Zayd would open their mouth and lose the thread, tracing the outline of the parking lot but unable to finish, leaving them frustrated and withdrawn. Zayd had come to believe that they could not rely on other people. The idea of depending on anyone felt like leaving a door unlocked. They had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. Their days narrowed into a loop of preparation and hesitation. Zayd used to be a happy person, but now they were always miserable, carrying a quiet exhaustion that no rest could touch. The avoidance and the compliance had reshaped their weeks. They started taking public transit an hour early, then skipped the morning rounds, leaving Leo to cover their notes. They accepted every last-minute shift swap from the clinic manager and apologized for breathing too loudly. By the time Zayd sat in the clinician’s office, the weight had become too heavy to carry alone. They had not come for a label, but because the mirror showed a stranger who flinched at slamming doors and who could no longer finish a sentence about the person who had taken their wallet. Zayd wanted to know how to stop waiting for the other shoe to drop, how to sit through a patient’s exam without their breath catching, and whether they could ever trust the quiet again. What they were most afraid of was that the vigilance would become permanent, and what they most hoped for was simply to breathe without counting the exits.
